title: The Story, Not the Story Teller
author: Hart, Nick
summary: Nick Hart argues that leadership storytelling is most powerful not when it radiates from a single heroic narrator but when it becomes co-constructed—a story people retell in their own words, argue with, and carry sideways through the organization. Drawing on Sally Maitlis's research on organizational sensemaking, Hart distinguishes public structure (assemblies, emails, CPD) from private structure (deliberate one-to-one conversations where the story is tested and rebuilt) and shows that both are necessary but that private conversations are what transform a story from one person's narrative into a shared reference point. Effective storytelling technique—naming conflict before resolution, leaving complications open, using concrete characters rather than abstract principles—creates gaps for other people's sensemaking to fill. The final move is to shift from 'leader as tag' (a person others follow) to 'story as tag' (a repeated, tested narrative that survives in places the leader was never in the room for).
points: Powerful storytelling can be learned, and when it is, the goal should be to make the story—not the teller—the recognized reference point that carries meaning through the organization.

Sally Maitlis's research shows that organizational sensemaking requires both leader-driven public structure and the organic, lateral retelling that happens in private conversations; without both, understanding stays thin.

Public structure (assemblies, emails, CPD) tells the story once at scale; private structure is where the story gets turned over, found wanting, rebuilt, and ultimately owned by people beyond the leader.
Opening with unresolved conflict—naming the tension before offering the answer—keeps the story live and creates the gap that invites other people's sensemaking to fill it.

The story becomes a self-organizing reference point when it has been tested in enough one-to-one conversations to survive contact with doubt and begins appearing in places the leader was never present.
quotes: powerful story telling can be learned and we can make it about the story, not the person.
The email goes out. The assembly happens. The CPD session runs, the story lands, heads nod. All of it well intentioned, all of it useful and all of it still one person’s story.
Leader input on its own produced something organised but flat. Meetings happened on schedule, the story got told in the right rooms, the language was consistent and the understanding stayed thin.
What was missing was energy; information moving sideways, people retelling the story in their own words, arguing with parts of it, co-constructing it.
A full windscreen but a quiet car can mean nobody’s actually arrived anywhere together.
Public structure tells the story once, at scale. Private structure is where the story actually gets handled, turned over, found wanting in places, and rebuilt.
A leader who opens with the decision already made (here’s what we’re doing and why) has closed the conflict before anyone else has had the chance to feel it.

The tag isn’t the leader. It’s the story, repeated often enough and tested in enough conversations that people start to recognise it on sight, in public and in private and begin to use it themselves to make sense of what’s happening around them.
What happens next is the part that decides whether that story mattered: whether it will be tested in enough one to one conversations to survive contact with other people’s doubts
